disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by one or more major depressive episodes accompanied by delusions and/or hallucinations that occur only during the depressive episode. The psychotic content is often mood-congruent, involving themes of guilt, worthlessness, or deserved punishment, though mood-incongruent psychotic features can also occur and generally indicate greater severity. The course can be episodic or recurrent, with substantial functional impairment in social, occupational, and self-care domains, and elevated risk of suicide. It is distinguished from primary psychotic disorders by the absence of psychosis outside of mood episodes and from bipolar disorder by the lack of past manic or hypomanic episodes.

narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Charleen ramped up her efforts to finish her GED and start CNA classes while still working irregular shifts as a personal care aide, often picking up extra hours to support her mother and younger cousins. The constant juggling of night shifts, exam prep, and volunteering at the youth center slowly eroded the routines that had kept her grounded—her Zumba crew, weekend hikes, and church activities became less frequent as she tried to “grind” her way toward nursing. Over time, she began falling behind in her coursework and making small documentation errors at work, which clashed sharply with her usual pride in being meticulous and dependable, and left her feeling singled out by supervisors and ashamed in front of her family and church community. When she started calling out of shifts, avoiding friends, and confiding to a trusted church elder that she was convinced she had already ruined her future and was being judged harshly by God and others, her pastor and an aunt insisted she see a mental health professional at a community clinic, leading to psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t shake this feeling that I’m a terrible person and that everything that’s gone wrong is my fault, like I’ve already messed up my whole life.”

narrative.stressor: Ross traces the beginning of his decline to a restructuring at his company about a year and a half ago, when his small, stable support team was downsized and he was left covering more users, on-call nights, and a complicated migration project with minimal backup. At first he coped by working late, spending weekends alone with his vinyl and Raspberry Pi projects, telling himself the pressure would ease once the new systems were in place, but instead the demands and his sense of responsibility kept increasing. Over the following year, he withdrew from board-game nights and photography outings, struggled to keep up with ticket queues and certification study, and began to feel that minor mistakes at work were catastrophic failures that might secretly be harming clients’ data and security. After he quietly used most of his savings on gear and travel he never enjoyed, stopped answering calls from friends, and confided to his sister during a visit that he was certain he was irreparably damaging the company and shouldn’t be trusted around computers at all, she persuaded him to see his primary care physician, who referred him urgently to psychiatry.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m convinced I’ve already ruined the company’s systems and that everyone will eventually find out I’m responsible for a huge disaster, even though people keep telling me everything is fine.”

narrative.stressor: Sharon’s difficulties began a little over a year ago, about six months after the sudden death of her husband from a heart attack, which upended the quiet, orderly life they had built in the Central Valley. Initially she coped by throwing herself into HR work, meditation, and solitary routines like gardening and birdwatching, telling colleagues she just needed time and space, but the house felt increasingly empty and her usual calming activities stopped bringing comfort. As the first anniversary of his death approached, she found it harder to maintain her usual steady presence at work, began declining hiking club outings and library shifts, and became preoccupied with the idea that she had missed subtle signs of his illness and somehow failed him by not insisting on more medical care. When her adult daughter noticed Sharon had stopped cooking, let her garden go to weeds, and was repeatedly saying that her husband’s death was “a punishment” for her past shortcomings and that she was certain she didn’t deserve to be alive when he wasn’t, the daughter accompanied her to their family doctor, who referred her for urgent psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since my husband died, it feels like this heavy sadness never lifts, like I’m stuck under it and can’t find any joy in anything anymore.”
